accroche: A demon tells you that you will live this life again, exactly as it is, without end. Nietzsche predicts nothing. He is testing you.
contenu_vulgarise:
*The Gay Science*, 1882, aphorism 341. Nietzsche gave it a title: “The Greatest Weight.”

A demon steals into your loneliest loneliness and says to you: this life, as you now live it and have lived it, you will have to live once more, an innumerable number of times. Nothing new; every pain, every joy, every thought, every sigh will return in the same order. The spider too. And this moonlight between the trees. And this very moment, and you yourself.

Then Nietzsche asks the only question that interests him: what would you do?

## It Is Not a Cosmology

Eternal recurrence is sometimes read as a thesis about the universe: time would be cyclical, everything would really repeat. Nietzsche sketched arguments of this kind in his notebooks, but that is not what aphorism 341 does.

The aphorism sets up a situation and observes your reaction. Two outcomes. You collapse, cursing the demon, a sign that you do not want this life. Or you answer that you have never heard anything more divine, which means you have stopped wanting anything other than what is.

Eternal recurrence is a measuring instrument. It does not describe the world; it gauges your relation to your own existence.

## Harder Than It Looks

The difficulty is not accepting the good moments. It is that the test is indivisible: everything returns, or nothing does. No selection, no correction. The humiliations, the bereavements, the botched decisions come back with the rest, identically, without end.

Saying yes to one's life under this condition therefore has nothing to do with satisfaction in front of a balance sheet. It means giving up the idea that the past should have been otherwise, which Nietzsche would name *amor fati*. Resignation endures what it laments. Amor fati is more demanding: to will what has taken place.

## What This Shifts

The test does not ask whether your life is successful by some external criterion. There is no grade, no jury, no retake.

It asks only whether you would take it back whole. Put this way, the question no longer concerns what you have accomplished so far, but what you are doing with your days, since they are what will return.

carte.punch: A demon tells you that you will live this life again, exactly as it is, without end.
carte.idee: Nietzsche predicts nothing. He is testing you. And the test is indivisible: everything returns, humiliations and bereavements included, with no possible correction. Saying yes is not being satisfied with your balance sheet. It is giving up wanting the past to have been otherwise.

quiz.question: What is eternal recurrence for in aphorism 341 of The Gay Science?
choix: To demonstrate that the time of the universe is structurally cyclical
To console the reader by promising that his joys will return one day
To prove that the past can no longer be changed once it has occurred
To test whether you would take back your whole life, removing nothing from it
quiz.explication: The aphorism advances no thesis about the structure of time: it sets up a situation and observes the reaction. The test lies in its indivisible character: everything returns, including what one would like to erase. It is therefore not a consolation, and the irreversibility of the past is not what is at stake, but the relation one has with it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What are the two possible reactions to the demon's announcement, according to the aphorism?
choix: Laughing off the joke, or questioning the demon's motives
Believing the demon at once, or demanding scientific proof
Collapsing while cursing him, or answering that one has never heard anything more divine
Thanking him for the warning, or asking him to change the past
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The aphorism provides for two outcomes: collapsing while cursing the demon, a sign that one does not want this life, or answering that one has never heard anything more divine, a sign that one has stopped wanting anything other than what is.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why is the test of eternal recurrence described as indivisible?
choix: Because it can be taken only once in a lifetime
Because everything returns or nothing does, with no possible selection or correction
Because it applies to humanity as a whole, never to an individual alone
Because Nietzsche never explains its meaning precisely
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The test is indivisible because no selection and no correction is possible: humiliations, bereavements, and botched decisions return with the rest, identically, without end.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does amor fati mean, as the entry defines it?
choix: To will what has taken place, rather than endure what one laments
A stoic indifference to everything that will happen next
The belief that everything happens for a preordained divine reason
An active refusal to accept what has already happened
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Amor fati is more demanding than resignation, which endures what it laments: it means giving up the idea that the past should have been otherwise, willing what has taken place.
